purpose: Original, public-safe seed patterns for generating new practice questions. These are generic templates, not copied course problems.

patterns.template: A finite collection has several labeled categories. Ask for the probability that one randomly selected item is not in one specified category.

variables.name: targetCount
variables.role: count in the excluded category

variables.name: otherCounts
variables.role: counts in all other categories

variables.name: categoryLabels
variables.role: neutral category names for the generated context

constraints: Use at least three categories.
Total count must be between 8 and 30.
The requested complement probability should simplify to a readable fraction.
generationNotes: Use a fresh everyday context such as tickets, cards, survey slips, or app icons.
Ask for one probability only.
Generate new counts and labels for each draft.
misconceptionHooks: Using the excluded category count as the numerator.
Using the wrong total count.
Forgetting that not A means total minus A.

patterns.template: A fixed set of distinct items is available. Ask for the number of unordered groups of a specified size.

variables.name: totalItems
variables.role: number of available distinct items

variables.name: groupSize
variables.role: number of items in the unordered group

variables.name: contextNoun
variables.role: neutral item type for the generated context

constraints: groupSize must be less than totalItems.
Wording must make order irrelevant.
Avoid extra restrictions beyond choosing the group.
generationNotes: Use C(n,k) as the intended formula.
Make clear that rearranging the same group does not create a new outcome.
Keep numbers small enough for manual simplification.
misconceptionHooks: Using permutations when order does not matter.
Forgetting to divide by repeated orderings.
Treating the group size as the number left out.

patterns.template: A group has a fixed number of distinct people or objects. Ask how many unordered selections of a specified size can be formed.

variables.name: totalItems
variables.role: number of available distinct items

variables.name: selectedItems
variables.role: number selected without order

variables.name: contextNoun
variables.role: neutral object or participant type

constraints: selectedItems must be less than totalItems.
Order must not matter in the wording.
Avoid restrictions that require inclusion-exclusion in this seed pattern.
generationNotes: Make the wording clearly about choosing a group, not arranging a sequence.
Use C(n,k) as the intended formula.
Keep numbers small enough for manual calculation.
misconceptionHooks: Using permutations when order does not matter.
Multiplying without dividing by repeated orderings.
Choosing the wrong value for k.

patterns.template: A fixed set of distinct items is available. Ask for the number of ordered sequences of a specified length formed without replacement.

variables.name: totalItems
variables.role: number of available distinct items

variables.name: orderedSlots
variables.role: number of ordered positions to fill

variables.name: contextNoun
variables.role: neutral item type for the generated context

constraints: orderedSlots must be less than totalItems.
Wording must make order matter.
Use distinct items and no replacement.
generationNotes: Use P(n,k) or an equivalent descending product.
Keep the product short enough for hand calculation.
Use a context where first, second, and later positions are meaningfully different.
misconceptionHooks: Using combinations when order matters.
Allowing repeated items even though the selection is without replacement.
Multiplying by too many or too few descending factors.

patterns.template: A rare or moderate-status group has one alert probability, while the complementary group has a different alert probability. Ask for the updated probability of the status given an alert.

variables.name: baseRate
variables.role: prior probability of the status of interest

variables.name: trueAlertRate
variables.role: probability of an alert when the status is present

variables.name: falseAlertRate
variables.role: probability of an alert when the status is absent

constraints: baseRate must be between 1% and 20%.
trueAlertRate must be larger than falseAlertRate.
The posterior probability should be neither near zero nor near one.
generationNotes: Use a public-safe alert or screening context with no medical diagnosis claims.
Compute the numerator and total alert probability explicitly.
Use project-owned wording for all solution steps.
misconceptionHooks: Confusing P(status given alert) with P(alert given status).
Ignoring the base rate.
Leaving out alerts from the complementary group.

patterns.template: A two-way table or grouped count is given. Ask for the probability of one attribute given that the selected item is already in a restricted group.

variables.name: conditionGroupCount
variables.role: number of items satisfying the given condition

variables.name: favorableWithinCondition
variables.role: number satisfying both the target event and condition

variables.name: outsideConditionCount
variables.role: number outside the condition, included only to tempt an incorrect denominator

constraints: favorableWithinCondition must be less than conditionGroupCount.
The correct denominator is conditionGroupCount, not the grand total.
The generated context should not require Bayes theorem.
generationNotes: Use neutral contexts such as survey responses, club signups, or transit choices.
Phrase the condition with 'given that' or equivalent wording.
Keep the table compact enough to inspect quickly.
misconceptionHooks: Using the full sample space after conditioning.
Confusing P(A | B) with P(B | A).
Counting items outside the condition.

patterns.template: Two independent events have stated probabilities. Ask for the probability that both events occur.

variables.name: firstProbability
variables.role: probability of the first independent event

variables.name: secondProbability
variables.role: probability of the second independent event

variables.name: eventContext
variables.role: neutral context where independence is plausible

constraints: The prompt must explicitly state the events are independent.
Ask for both events occurring, not either event.
Product probability should be between 0.02 and 0.80.
generationNotes: Use decimal or percent answers consistently.
Do not introduce conditional wording.
Use contexts where independence sounds natural and simple.
misconceptionHooks: Adding probabilities instead of multiplying.
Treating independent events as mutually exclusive.
Forgetting to convert percents to decimals before multiplying.

patterns.template: A discrete random variable has a small set of values and probabilities. Ask for the expected value as a probability-weighted average.

variables.name: outcomeValues
variables.role: possible numeric outcomes

variables.name: probabilities
variables.role: probabilities assigned to all outcomes

variables.name: contextNoun
variables.role: neutral source of the payoff or score

constraints: Use three or four outcomes.
Probabilities must sum to 1.
Expected value should be a readable decimal or fraction.
generationNotes: Present the values and probabilities in a compact table or sentence.
Ask for expected value only.
Write fresh solution steps that multiply each value by its probability.
misconceptionHooks: Averaging outcomes without probability weights.
Treating expected value as the most likely value.
Forgetting one outcome in the weighted sum.

patterns.template: A discrete random variable has several values and probabilities. Ask for the variance using the probability-weighted spread from the mean.

variables.name: outcomeValues
variables.role: possible numeric outcomes

variables.name: probabilities
variables.role: probabilities assigned to all outcomes

variables.name: contextNoun
variables.role: neutral count or score being modeled

constraints: Use three or four outcomes.
Probabilities must sum to 1.
Variance should be a readable decimal.
generationNotes: Compute the mean first.
Use E(X^2) - [E(X)]^2 or equivalent weighted squared deviations.
Keep values small enough for hand-checkable arithmetic.
misconceptionHooks: Reporting the mean instead of the variance.
Averaging squared deviations without probability weights.
Subtracting the mean instead of the mean squared.

patterns.template: A fixed number of independent trials has the same success probability on each trial. Ask for the probability of exactly a specified number of successes.

variables.name: trialCount
variables.role: number of independent trials

variables.name: successCount
variables.role: exact number of successes

variables.name: successProbability
variables.role: same probability of success on each trial

constraints: successCount must be between 1 and trialCount minus 1.
Trials must be independent with a constant success probability.
Reject cases with extremely tiny or near-certain final probabilities.
generationNotes: Use C(n,k)p^k(1-p)^(n-k) as the intended formula.
Use contexts involving repeated attempts, checks, messages, or prompts.
Keep n small enough for hand-checkable arithmetic.
misconceptionHooks: Forgetting the combination factor.
Using k as the number of failures.
Adding p repeatedly instead of multiplying powers.

patterns.template: A finite population contains two item types. A sample is drawn without replacement. Ask for the probability of exactly a specified number of one item type in the sample.

variables.name: populationSize
variables.role: total number of items in the population

variables.name: successItems
variables.role: number of items of the target type

variables.name: drawCount
variables.role: number of items sampled without replacement

variables.name: observedSuccesses
variables.role: exact number of target items in the sample

constraints: successItems must be less than populationSize.
observedSuccesses must not exceed successItems or drawCount.
drawCount minus observedSuccesses must not exceed the number of non-target items.
generationNotes: Use C(successItems, observedSuccesses) times C(otherItems, otherDraws) over C(populationSize, drawCount).
Make the without-replacement condition explicit.
Keep the denominator small enough for a readable fraction or four-decimal answer.
misconceptionHooks: Using a binomial model even though sampling is without replacement.
Counting only the target items and ignoring the non-target selections.
Using the population size as the sample size.

patterns.template: A binomial count has a moderately large number of trials and success probability. Ask for an approximate tail probability using a normal model with continuity correction.

variables.name: trialCount
variables.role: number of Bernoulli trials

variables.name: successProbability
variables.role: success probability for each trial

variables.name: thresholdCount
variables.role: count used in the tail event

variables.name: continuityAdjustment
variables.role: half-unit adjustment used before standardizing

constraints: Both np and n(1-p) should be at least 10.
The threshold should be within about three standard deviations of the mean.
Use a continuity correction for inclusive count wording.
generationNotes: Compute mu = np and sigma = sqrt(np(1-p)).
Convert the corrected count to a z-score.
Report an approximate probability using a standard normal table or calculator.
misconceptionHooks: Forgetting the continuity correction.
Using p as the standard deviation instead of sqrt(np(1-p)).
Using the wrong tail after standardizing.
